strengths: The central reformulation of data selection as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP (Definition 3.2/3.1) with an explicit objective averaging utility over all selection budgets is clean, well-motivated, and gives quantitative meaning to the informal 'selection curve' evaluation used across the data valuation literature.

Theorem 4.1 provides a genuinely useful unifying lens: semi-value methods (Data Shapley, Beta Shapley, Data Banzhaf) are shown to be myopic policies on a linear reward surrogate, with a correct proof via least-squares value recovery and myopic-policy equivalence (Appendix C). This yields interpretable explanations for when these methods succeed (Theorem 4.3, linear utilities) and fail (Remark 4.7, high curvature).

The curvature analysis (Theorem 4.6 and Appendix E) extends known (1-c)-style submodular approximation bounds to the sequential selection objective, and the empirical curvature experiment (Appendix I, Figures 5-6) is a thoughtful controlled design that qualitatively confirms the predicted degradation and method convergence at high substitutability.

Evaluating against an exact dynamic-programming oracle (Algorithm 1) on small datasets directly quantifies how far existing valuation methods are from sequential optimality, which is a valuable diagnostic absent from prior work.
The paper is generally well written, with a clear three-part decomposition (reward modeling vs. decision policy) and honest positioning against parallel work (Appendix A.3).
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is moderate. Theorem 4.1 largely repackages the known least-squares characterization of semi-values (Li & Yu, 2024, which the authors cite) plus a trivial myopic-policy step, and Theorem 4.6/E.3 adapts standard curvature-based greedy analysis (Balkanski et al., 2016) to the summed objective; the claim of being 'the first systematic framework' is overstated given prior data-selection-as-submodular-optimization work.

The proposed bipartite surrogate method is ad hoc: edges are learned by thresholding feature distances with a grid search, all weights are set to 1, and the central guarantee (greedy is optimal when the surrogate is 'correctly specified and learned', Theorem G.3) holds only under an unverifiable condition. The proof of Theorem G.3 via an exchange/inversion argument is sketchy — e.g., the claim that any inversion-free sequence must coincide with greedy needs a more careful argument.

Experiments are small-scale and narrow: only 20-100 training points, a single target model (logistic regression), and OpenML tabular datasets. The exact-DP comparison is only feasible at n=20, and the practical value of the bipartite method in modern deep-learning selection settings (the motivating application area) is not demonstrated. No ablations on surrogate quality, threshold sensitivity, or computational cost of the graph-learning procedure.

The empirical curvature validation never actually measures the curvature c; propagation proportion is used as a qualitative proxy, so the claimed alignment with the (1-c)^2 bound is not quantitatively verified.

Presentation defects undermine confidence: Table 1's Average/Std Dev rows are clearly erroneous (0.255/0.043 averages across accuracies of ~0.5-0.9), inconsistent algorithm/section numbering (Algorithm 1 vs. 'Algorithm B', references to 'Section 4.4' that does not exist in the main text), a malformed constraint in Appendix C.1 (Û(S)θi), typos ('preforms'), and a reference in Section 5.2 to 'two approximation approaches' that is never clarified.
No explicit limitations discussion, no mention of code release, and reproducibility is limited given the underspecified graph-learning details (number of thresholds, subset size k, etc.).

strengths: The core reframing of ranking-based data selection as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP, and the observation that game-theoretic semi-values correspond to myopic policies over linear surrogate utilities (Theorem 4.1), is a clean conceptual lens that connects data valuation to the approximate dynamic programming literature.

The curvature-based analysis (Theorem 4.6 / Appendix E) provides a plausible explanation, aligned with prior empirical findings, for why semi-value methods degrade on datasets with high substitutability, and the RQ2 experiment is a reasonable attempt to test this mechanism in a controlled setting.

The paper is generally well-motivated, positions itself against a clear evaluation protocol (selection curves across budgets), and builds on standard benchmarks and the OpenDataVal infrastructure, which aids comparability and reproducibility.
The attempt to derive an explicit, budget-agnostic objective (Definition 3.2) for what 'good data values for selection' means is a useful formalization step that prior work has left implicit.
weaknesses: Direct contradiction between claims and the paper's own evidence: Section 7.3 and Appendix J state that 'Bipartite achieves the highest accuracy across all datasets,' yet Table 1 shows BetaShap (0.747) outperforming Bipartite (0.745) on 2dplanes. Such overclaiming undermines trust in the empirical analysis.

Table 1 is internally inconsistent/garbled: the 'Average' row lists DataShap at 0.043, DVRL at 0.041, and Bipartite at 0.041 while all other methods show ~0.25, which is irreconcilable with the per-dataset accuracies (~0.4-0.88) reported above it. This suggests careless or buggy reporting of a central result.

Limited significance and scale of experiments: the 'optimal' DP comparison (RQ1) uses only 20 training points, and the bipartite evaluation uses 50-100 training points with logistic regression. The central claims about closing the gap to optimal selection are validated only in a regime far removed from practical data selection (thousands to millions of points, deep models), making 'extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness across diverse datasets' an overstatement.

The theoretical contribution is largely incremental. The (1-c)^2 greedy bound under curvature builds directly on classical curvature analysis of greedy submodular maximization (which the authors acknowledge via Balkanski et al. 2016), and the linear-utility optimality result (Theorem 4.3) is essentially immediate. The unification (Theorem 4.1) relies on the weighted-least-squares view of semi-values already established by Li & Yu (2024), and Lemma C.1's 'proof' via the law of large numbers is hand-wavy, ignoring finite-sample approximation error in the trajectory equivalence.

A gap between theory and method: the bipartite surrogate's guarantee (Theorem G.3) only says greedy is optimal under the surrogate when the surrogate is correctly specified, which is untestable in practice and says nothing about optimality w.r.t. the ground-truth utility. The bipartite construction itself is a fairly ad-hoc similarity-thresholded coverage heuristic whose threshold is tuned using ground-truth utilities obtained via actual model training, weakening the claimed computational-efficiency advantage; no runtime or cost comparison is provided.

The RQ2 'validation' of the (1-c)^2 guarantee never measures curvature c; it uses a message-passing proxy and reports only that accuracy drops from ~0.74 to ~0.59, which is qualitative and does not verify the specific quadratic bound claimed.

The proof of Theorem G.3 (greedy optimality for the cumulative objective) is sketchy: the inversion-swapping argument does not rigorously establish termination at the greedy sequence, since marginal gains must be re-evaluated after each swap and tie-breaking is not addressed.

Presentation sloppiness throughout: cross-references are broken or inconsistent (e.g., 'Section 4.4' and 'Algorithm B' do not match the actual numbering; 'Definition 3.2' is referred to as 'Problem 3.2'), the constrained least-squares formulation in Appendix C.1 is garbled ('U(S)θ_i = U(D) − U(∅)'), and there is no dedicated limitations discussion despite substantial scope restrictions (tiny datasets, linear/greedy guarantees, surrogate-dependence).

strengths: The core reframing is appealing: casting value-based data selection as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP whose solution induces a ranking covering all budgets k is a clean, explicit formalization of what existing selection-curve evaluation protocols only implicitly assume.

Theorem 4.1, showing that game-theoretic data values (Data Shapley, Beta Shapley, Data Banzhaf) correspond to myopic policies over a weighted-least-squares linear surrogate, is a genuinely useful unifying lens, connecting the data valuation literature to ADP and to prior least-squares utility-learning work.

The curvature analysis (Theorem 4.6, Remark 4.7) yields an interpretable (1-c)^2 guarantee for semi-value-based ranking and a plausible explanation for the empirically observed weakness of Data Shapley on homogeneous/substitutable data; the controlled message-passing experiment (Appendix I) that varies curvature is a nice validation design.

The RQ1 experiments comparing existing methods against an exact dynamic-programming oracle on small datasets meaningfully quantify the gap between standard values and optimal sequential selection, which is an informative contribution beyond method comparison alone.
The paper is generally well organized, with complete proofs, algorithms, and detailed experimental settings in the appendix, supporting reproducibility of the reported results.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim of the proposed method — that greedy selection under the learned bipartite coverage surrogate is optimal (Theorem G.3, and the abstract's 'ensuring greedy selection is still optimal') — appears incorrect. Greedy is not optimal for maximum-coverage (or capacity-constrained coverage) objectives; it achieves only (1-1/e)-type approximation. The exchange-argument proof in Appendix G.4 is sketchy and glosses over exactly the step (that 'a sequence with no inversions must be the greedy sequence') where the argument fails for general submodular coverage functions. This is a material soundness problem for the paper's main methodological contribution.

The (1-c)^2 guarantee of Theorem 4.6 is essentially an application of known curvature-based bounds from submodular maximization (the paper itself cites Balkanski et al., 2016 as inspiration), so the theoretical novelty here is modest: the main technical theorems are either reinterpretations of existing least-squares/valuation results (C.1 closely follows Li & Yu, 2024 and Wang et al., 2024b) or adaptations of classical submodular analysis.

All experiments are at very small scale (20-100 training points, 50-100 validation points, logistic regression only, tabular OpenML datasets). The DP oracle is only feasible at n=20, and the bipartite method is never compared against the oracle (Figure 4 omits DynamicProgramming), so the 'near-optimal' claim of the surrogate is asserted theoretically but never verified empirically at any scale where both can run. No experiments with deep models or realistic data-selection budgets are provided, which limits the significance of the claims for the data-selection community.

The bipartite surrogate itself is a fairly heuristic KNN/label-matching coverage construction (feature-distance threshold plus label agreement, threshold tuned on sampled subsets), with no ablations on its sensitivity, no comparison to simpler diversity/coverage selection baselines (e.g., KNN-centered methods, k-center, or Data Shapley with learned utilities as in Wang et al., 2021), which weakens attribution of the gains to the ADP framing rather than to generic coverage-based selection.

Presentation and internal consistency issues: the proof of Lemma C.1 contains a nonsensical constraint ('Û(S)θ_i = U(D) − U(∅)'); the text references 'Section 4.4' which does not exist; Section 5.2 mentions 'our two approximation approaches' without defining them; Table 1's Average/Std Dev rows are inconsistent with the data (averages of ~0.7 accuracies reported as 0.255/0.043); and typos such as 'preforms' remain. Section 6 (value functions) adds little beyond defining v*(i) = n - t*(i), i.e., the rank in the optimal trajectory.

There is no limitations section and no discussion of when the bipartite approximation is expected to fail (e.g., non-monotone utility, model capacity effects, feature-similarity being a poor proxy for utility influence), even though the framework's assumptions (monotone submodularity, coverage-structured utility) are strong and known to be violated by practical model-training utilities.

strengths: The sequential decision-making reformulation of data selection is clean and well-executed: the DMDP formulation (Problem 3.1, Section 3.1) with prefix-utility rewards exactly matches the area-under-selection-curve objective, and the paper is unusually transparent about terminology (Remark 3.2 admits its 'ADP' framing is really 'surrogate model + myopic policy') and about the scope of its claims (Remark D.3 on LOO, Remark G.5 on the worst-case nature of the bound, Remark H.3 on the idealized sandwich conditions).

Theorem 4.1's regression characterizations (Shapley as constrained WLS per KernelSHAP, Banzhaf as unconstrained OLS with centered features, Beta Shapley as weighted OLS under Beta sampling) are assembled with care, and the paper correctly identifies the efficiency-axiom distinction that determines which regression form applies, including the well-definedness caveats in Remark D.1.

The experimental evaluation is unusually comprehensive and honest: DP-based optimality verification against nine baselines (Table 1), a controlled substitutability/curvature experiment (RQ2) that explicitly disclaims direct curvature estimation, utility-approximation error analysis (Table 3), a Budget-500 protocol with careful accounting of ties and per-method averaging, and a real large-scale DATE-LM LLM evaluation (Tables 6-8) with ablations over embedding backends and full cost reporting (Table 5).

The paper engages seriously with parallel/related work (GraphFilter, datamodels/DsDm, sequential submodular optimization, optimization-from-samples) and clearly delineates what is new, e.g., the (1-c)^2 ranking bound vs. the greedy curvature bounds of Balkanski et al.

Reproducibility appears strong: code is stated to be public, baselines use the standardized OpenDataVal implementations, and hyperparameters, seeds, splits, and computational budgets are documented in detail (Appendix J).
weaknesses: The core theoretical contributions are relatively incremental. The DMDP formulation and Bellman equation are straightforward; Theorem 4.2 (data values as myopic ADP policies) is essentially definitional since linear surrogates have state-independent marginal gains; Theorem 4.3 follows immediately from Lemma F.2; and the (1-c)^2 bound of Theorem 4.4 is a modest extension of standard curvature analysis (and is weaker than the (1-c)/(1+c-c^2) greedy bound of Balkanski et al., 2016 that the authors themselves cite). The 'unifying' framing is thus more of a reinterpretation than a technically deep synthesis.

The bipartite coverage surrogate is a fairly classical similarity-based set-cover/facility-location objective with a tuned distance threshold. Its connection to the sequential framework is loose: the practical method reduces to submodular greedy on a coverage surrogate, and the paper lacks ablations isolating whether the gains come from coverage/diversity per se (compare against plain facility-location or GraphFilter-style baselines under identical embeddings and threshold tuning) rather than from the proposed framework.

The end-to-end guarantee (Theorem H.2) rests on uniform multiplicative sandwich conditions that the authors themselves concede are 'typically too strong' and unverified; the practical claim is downgraded to an empirical one, so the method's theoretical guarantee does not actually cover the deployed algorithm.

Classical-ML experiments are small-scale: 20-50 training points for the DP-optimality comparison and 50-100 training points for the main selection curves with logistic regression targets. The DP 'optimal' benchmark is only meaningful at this tiny scale, which weakens how far the RQ1 gap findings (8.4-23.8%) generalize to realistic selection problems.

The curvature-to-substitutability link in RQ2 is qualitative ('we use substitutability as a qualitative proxy'), so the empirical validation of Theorem 4.4 is suggestive rather than quantitative, and the consistency claims (e.g., convergence of methods at high substitutability) are fairly weak tests of the theory.

The LLM result improvement over RDS+ (+1.01% average) is modest, and the authors' own footnote acknowledges potential label leakage inherent to the DATE-LM reference construction; also, coverage saturated after only 1-5 selections in practice, so the deployed BipCov is largely mean-similarity fallback, somewhat diluting the coverage story in that setting.

strengths: The paper asks a well-motivated and underexplored question: what is the optimization objective that data values are implicitly serving during selection, and when do value-based rankings fail? Framing the selection curve (AUSC) as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP is a clean lens, and the reinterpretation of semi-values as myopic greedy policies under linear surrogates is a genuinely useful unifying viewpoint.

The writing is clear and well organized, and the paper is unusually honest about the limits of its claims: Remark 3.2 admits the ADP terminology is a stretch, Remark G.5 concedes the (1-c)^2 bound is worst-case and mainly explanatory, and Remark H.3 concedes the sandwich conditions in Theorem H.2 'may fail for coverage surrogates' so the end-to-end guarantee is largely idealized.

The appendix theory (regression characterizations via centered features in Theorem 4.1, curvature analysis in Appendix G, the submodularity proof for the coverage surrogate in Appendix H.1) is correct-looking, self-contained, and careful about scope (e.g., the LOO discussion in Remark D.3 and Appendix D).

The empirical comparison against an exact DP-optimal selector (Table 1), while only possible at small scale, is a novel and interesting diagnostic that quantifies real headroom (8-24%) for existing valuation methods.
The DATE-LM evaluation follows the official benchmark pipeline with multiple seeds, ablations over embedding backends, and reasonable computational-cost reporting.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty. Theorem 4.1 largely restates known results (KernelSHAP/Lundberg & Lee 2017; Charnes et al. 1988). Theorem 4.2 is nearly tautological (linear surrogates have state-independent marginal gains, so greedy = sorting by values). Theorem 4.3 is a direct corollary of Lemma F.2. Theorem 4.4's (1-c)^2 bound is loose and straightforward; the related (1-c)/(1+c-c^2) result of Balkanski et al. (2016) cited in Appendix A.5 is in fact tighter for the range of relevant c, weakening the claim of a new analysis.

The headline 'end-to-end' guarantee (Theorem H.2) rests on uniform sandwich conditions the authors themselves state cannot be verified and may fail in practice (Remark H.3); condition (ii) is explicitly 'not guaranteed in general' for coverage surrogates. The practical method therefore has essentially no non-vacuous guarantee, despite the abstract advertising 'provable guarantees'.

The bipartite coverage surrogate is conceptually close to existing set-cover/similarity-graph selection methods (GraphFilter, Wu et al. 2025, acknowledged as parallel work; DsDm/datamodels for linear surrogates), and the DATE-LM result undercuts the coverage story: binary coverage saturates after 2, 1, and 5 selections (Appendix J.7.2), so nearly the entire 10k ranking is a mean-similarity fallback. The reported gain over RDS+ is ~1% average, and BipCov is actually worse than RDS+ on BBH (66.27 vs 66.80).

Experimental scale undermines the central RQ1/RQ3 claims: the DP-optimality comparison uses only 20 training points and 100 validation points, with very high variance (e.g., digits optimal 0.177 +/- 0.213; several cells with +/- 0.2-0.3); selection budgets are 50-100 points. It is unclear the 8-24% gaps or the Bipartite advantages persist at realistic dataset sizes or with models beyond logistic regression.

The curvature validation (RQ2) never measures curvature c; it uses a qualitative 'substitutability' proxy from message passing. The observed degradation is consistent with the theory but does not discriminate it from many alternative explanations, so the empirical support for Theorem 4.4 is weak.

The ADP framing adds conceptual weight more than technical content: as Remark 3.2 concedes, the framework reduces to 'surrogate model + myopic policy', and the MDP construction is a standard restatement of greedy prefix optimization. The claimed 'unification' is thus largely a repackaging of known greedy/linear-surrogate equivalences.

Reproducibility concerns: the abstract's code URL is incomplete/empty ('Code is publicly available at' with no link), and no artifact is verifiable from the manuscript; the RQ2 controlled framework and the DP baseline are non-standard and described only in appendices.

Some presentation/protocol inconsistencies: Table 1 reports only 'Optimal DP' and 'Best Baseline' per dataset (the best baseline differs per dataset, making the comparison selectively favorable), the Budget-500 protocol differs from the curve protocol in ways that complicate cross-referencing, and the date-election/ties footnotes obscure significance of wins.

strengths: The sequential decision-making formulation of data selection (Problem 3.1, DMDP with prefix-utility rewards) is clean and gives a principled optimization target that existing ranking-by-value protocols only implicitly optimize.

The reinterpretation of game-theoretic data values as myopic linear surrogates within approximate dynamic programming is a genuinely useful conceptual lens, and the paper is honest about the terminology (Remark 3.2) and about the scope of its unification (Remark D.3, LOO caveats).
The curvature analysis (Theorem 4.4, Appendix G) gives a worst-case explanation for when ranking-based selection degrades, and the RQ2 experiments are designed to probe this prediction qualitatively.

The experimental coverage is broad: eight OpenML datasets with 20 independent runs, comparison against nine baselines via OpenDataVal, utility-approximation error analysis (Table 3), and an additional large-scale LLM fine-tuning evaluation on the DATE-LM benchmark with careful protocol details (Appendix J.7) and measured computational costs (Table 5).

Limitations are discussed unusually candidly: the sandwich conditions of Theorem H.2 are explicitly flagged as idealized and possibly violated (Remark H.3), the coverage saturation in the DATE-LM experiments is disclosed (Appendix J.7.2), and the (1-c)^2 bound is framed as worst-case and 'most useful for explaining failures rather than predicting success.'
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. Theorem 4.1's regression characterizations largely restate known results (KernelSHAP, Charnes et al. 1988), Theorem 4.2 is nearly immediate (any linear surrogate makes myopic greedy equivalent to value ranking), and Theorem 4.3 is trivial for linear utilities. The (1-c)^2 bound is also weaker than the existing (1-c)/(1+c-c^2) curvature bound the paper itself cites (Balkanski et al., 2016), so the new theoretical content is thin.

The bipartite coverage surrogate is a standard coverage/facility-location-style submodular function with greedy selection; the related GraphFilter work (Wu et al., 2025) already uses bipartite-graph greedy selection for LLM SFT. The end-to-end guarantee (Theorem H.2) depends on sandwich conditions the authors admit do not hold in practice, so the method's theoretical support reduces to submodularity of a hand-crafted surrogate.

The headline LLM claim is undercut by the paper's own disclosure: binary coverage saturates after 2, 1, and 5 selections on MMLU/GSM8K/BBH, meaning BipCov behaves almost entirely as mean-similarity fallback over the 10k budget. The resulting gain over RDS+ (+1.01%) is small relative to seed-level variation and does not strongly validate the coverage mechanism.

The classical-ML experiments use very small training pools (20 points for RQ1 DP verification, 50-100 for RQ3), limiting the evidence that the framework matters at realistic data-selection scales; the DP 'optimal' baseline is only computable in this regime.
The curvature-impact experiments (RQ2) use substitutability as only a qualitative proxy and do not measure the actual curvature c, so the empirical connection to Theorem 4.4 remains loose.

The unification claim ('unifies existing methods') is somewhat oversold given the explicit exceptions (LOO, general game-theoretic values in Remark D.3), and the practical method inherits little from the sequential framework beyond greedy selection on a surrogate.
